title: Against Meritocracy
abstract: Meritocracy today involves the idea that whatever your social position at birth, society ought to offer enough opportunity and mobility for ‘talent’ to combine with ‘effort’ in order to ‘rise to the top’. This idea is one of the most prevalent social and cultural tropes of our time, as palpable in the speeches of politicians as in popular culture. In this book Jo Littler argues that meritocracy is the key cultural means of legitimation for contemporary neoliberal culture – and that whilst it promises opportunity, it in fact creates new forms of social division. Against Meritocracy is split into two parts. Part I explores the genealogies of meritocracy within social theory, political discourse and working cultures. It traces the dramatic U-turn in meritocracy’s meaning, from socialist slur to a contemporary ideal of how a society should be organised. Part II uses a series of case studies to analyse the cultural pull of popular ‘parables of progress’, from reality TV to the super-rich and celebrity CEOs, from social media controversies to the rise of the ‘mumpreneur’. Paying special attention to the role of gender, ‘race’ and class, this book provides new conceptualisations of the meaning of meritocracy in contemporary culture and society.

Full narrative

Against Meritocracy by Jo Littler was published by Taylor & Francis in 2017. Conceptually, the work connects to Meritocracy, Political science and Law.

OpenAlex records 319 citations. That places it in the top 1% of works in its field and year of publication. Citations peaked in 2023 with 42 citing works. Notable citing venues include European Journal of Cultural Studies, Cambridge University Press eBooks and Feminist Media Studies. Of 62 citation statements scite has classified, 1 support its claims, 52 mention it in passing, and none contradict it. The citing works include 242 journal articles and 52 book chapters. They come from 40 countries, led by the United Kingdom, the United States and Australia. The citation record includes 1 formal book review.

narrative_llm:
Short impact summary

Jo Littler’s Against Meritocracy has become a widely cited reference point in debates about merit, inequality, and neoliberal legitimation. The book has 319 OpenAlex citations, placing it in the top 1% of works for its field and year, alongside nearly 10,000 recorded OAPEN downloads and a small but visible footprint in public and educational use, including a Wikipedia citation, a formal book review, and a recorded talk that explicitly links to the book.

Full narrative

Against Meritocracy argues that meritocracy is not a neutral principle of fair competition but a key cultural mechanism through which contemporary neoliberalism justifies inequality. That argument has travelled strongly across scholarly literature: the book is cited in sociology, education, cultural studies, media studies, and related fields, with especially strong uptake in journal articles and book chapters. The citation record shows sustained attention over time, with recent citing works continuing to frame meritocracy in relation to legitimacy, social mobility, gender, education, and cultural recognition.

The citing landscape suggests that the book has been used less as a narrow specialist source than as a conceptual anchor for broader syntheses. It appears most often in education-focused work, but also in scholarship on feminism and media, social policy, cultural industries, and welfare. The venues citing it include established interdisciplinary journals such as the European Journal of Cultural Studies, Feminist Media Studies, and the British Journal of Sociology, indicating that the book’s core argument has resonated across overlapping humanities and social-science conversations. The work’s citation base is geographically broad as well, with the strongest concentration in the United Kingdom and additional use in the United States, Australia, Germany, Canada, and elsewhere.

Usage signals complement the citation record. The book has nearly 10,000 OAPEN downloads, pointing to substantial reader interest in an open-access format, and the monthly pattern shows continuing uptake rather than a one-time spike. Library and discovery data also indicate circulation in academic collections, and the book appears in a YouTube recording from The Sociological Review Foundation, suggesting use in teaching or public scholarly discussion. A single Wikipedia citation to the “myth of meritocracy” page adds a modest sign of public discourse beyond the academy.

Other signals point to durable scholarly and reader-facing visibility. There is one formal book review in the record, and reader-platform traces on sites such as Goodreads, Amazon, and LibraryThing indicate commercial and community discovery, though these are not the same as scholarly uptake. Overall, the record shows a book with strong academic influence, clear interdisciplinary reach, and meaningful open-access readership, especially around debates on social mobility, legitimacy, power, and the politics of inequality.
